Combined Arms
Combined arms refers to the synchronized and simultaneous application of arms to achieve an effect greater than separate use.<SEP>Combined arms advantages are exploited to the maximum possible extent in hasty operations.

ADP 3-90
ADP 3-90 is a military doctrine publication dated 31 July 2019 that outlines tactical fundamentals and the science of tactics.<SEP>ADP 3-90 is a document dated 31 July 2019 discussing tactical fundamentals.<SEP>ADP 3-90 is the primary publication for the offense and defense at the tactical level, providing authoritative guidance.<SEP>ADP 3-90 is the manual containing the text regarding tactics, operations, and risk.<SEP>A doctrinal publication dated 31 July 2019 containing tactical fundamentals and risk reduction factors.<SEP>ADP 3-90 is a document containing doctrine regarding command and the operations process.

Combined Arms Team
A combined arms team is a formation that uses combined arms through synchronized application of elements.

Warfighting Functions
Warfighting functions are the last six elements of combat power described by the Army.

ADP 3-0
ADP 3-0 is a referenced military doctrine publication that defines combined arms and combat power.<SEP>ADP 3-0 defines defeat as rendering a force incapable of achieving its objectives.<SEP>ADP 3-0 is referenced for discussions on strategic and operational levels and the definition of defeat.<SEP>ADP 3-0 provides additional information on the consolidation of gains.<SEP>ADP 3-0 provides information on irregular warfare and distinguishes it from conventional warfare.<SEP>A referenced document providing information on Army tenets of operations and principles of war.<SEP>ADP 3-0 is a referenced document providing further details on the imperatives of Army operations.

Army
The Army is the military organization that collectively describes warfighting functions and trains leaders for tactical situations.<SEP>Army forces operate in more than just the land domain and depend on affecting enemy behavior.<SEP>The Army utilizes capabilities and doctrines such as ADP 3-90 for tactical operations.<SEP>The Army is a military branch whose involvement in counterterrorism is limited by Department of Defense directives.<SEP>The Army follows an organizational approach for multidomain operations and joint operations.<SEP>The Army is a military organization that utilizes imperatives to align efforts and maintain advantage over adversaries.

Science of Tactics
The science of tactics involves understanding measurable military aspects like capabilities, techniques, and procedures.<SEP>The science of tactics is the understanding of military aspects that can be measured and codified.

Combat Power
Combat power is the total means of destructive, constructive, and information capabilities a unit can apply at a given time.<SEP>Combat power is concentrated at the decisive point to place an enemy in a disadvantageous position.<SEP>The capability of friendly forces that commanders seek to preserve and concentrate against enemy vulnerabilities.

Enemy Forces
Enemy forces are opposing units whose decision-making abilities commanders seek to disrupt and degrade.<SEP>Enemy forces are opposing groups with goals that commanders seek to defeat.<SEP>Enemy forces are opposing forces that tacticians develop solutions against.<SEP>Enemy forces are opposed by commanders and create uncertainty in the operational environment.<SEP>Hostile groups establishing positions and ambush sites in urban areas.

Offensive Action
Offensive action is key to achieving decisive results and is normally required for tactical success.

Momentum
Momentum complements initiative and reflects a unit's combat power and operational tempo.<SEP>Momentum complements and helps maintain the initiative, reflecting a unit's combat power and operational tempo.

Leaders
Leaders train for tactical situations, master the science of tactics, and develop decision-making abilities through education and experience.<SEP>Leaders need creativity and clarity to make decisions under uncertainty and act decisively.<SEP>Leaders require critical skills in tactics and understanding commander's intent.

Decisive Results
Decisive results are the outcome achieved through offensive action and accomplishing missions.

31 July 2019
31 July 2019 is the publication date associated with ADP 3-90.

Commanders
Commanders are leaders responsible for defeating adversary forces and accomplishing missions that support operational or strategic purposes. They apply principles and imperatives to achieve objectives, developing operations and selecting how to employ force discriminately. Their actions are considered strategic, operational, or tactical based on whether they achieve corresponding objectives. To succeed, Commanders apply tactics, balance risk, and maintain initiative, seeking to initiate combat on favorable terms.

Commanders are responsible for maintaining momentum and making critical decisions while training subordinates in tactical operations. They must weigh information, uncertainty, risk, and available forces against the disposition of the main body to achieve their purpose. Additionally, Commanders face specific challenges in enabling collaboration and assuring access within contested environments. Through these multifaceted responsibilities, they strive to fulfill their role in achieving objectives and defeating enemies.

Friendly Forces
Friendly Forces encompass military units, personnel, capabilities, organizations, and materiel operating under command to seize the initiative. These forces are protected and sustained by commanders during and after battles, requiring agility, protection, and responsive support throughout operations. Success for Friendly Forces is determined by winning battles based on the outcomes of engagements, necessitating a robust structure capable of facing complex threats from opposing forces.

Coordination is vital, as Friendly Forces are managed by commanders who facilitate information sharing through the operations process. Military personnel within these groups require synchronization and communication to maintain effectiveness. Specific operational safety protocols dictate that personnel must be alerted of impending dangers by aircraft. Furthermore, in complex settings such as urban environments, Friendly Forces employ SUAS operations to navigate threats and maintain operational advantage.

Course of Action
A course of action (COA) is developed to address specific tactical problems and represents a choice among options.<SEP>A plan or option evaluated by commanders, where the best COA may involve the greatest risk.

Initiative
Initiative allows commanders to make the enemy react and maintain control over the tempo of operations.<SEP>The initiative is a key operational state that friendly forces seek to seize, retain, and exploit against enemy forces.

Limit of Advance
A specific point where offensive action ends when forces reach it.

Rules of Engagement
Regulations that impose constraints on friendly and enemy force capabilities.

Terrain
Physical ground that leaders learn to employ to their advantage and commanders seek to control.

Leadership
One of the eight elements of combat power.

Information
One of the eight elements of combat power.<SEP>Current and accurate data accessed by systems to support commander understanding and decision-making.<SEP>Information is a factor continually weighed by Commanders alongside uncertainty and risk.

Command and Control
One of the eight elements of combat power.

Movement and Maneuver
One of the eight elements of combat power.

Intelligence
One of the eight elements of combat power.

Cyberspace Operations
Cyberspace operations are capabilities integrated by friendly forces to affect enemy capabilities.<SEP>Activities conducted to isolate and degrade enemy decision-making abilities.

Fires
One of the eight elements of combat power and used to destroy critical enemy capabilities.

Sustainment
One of the eight elements of combat power.

Staffs
Staffs provide input to commanders and assist in the military decision-making process.<SEP>Staffs advise Commanders in determining optimal formation and organization.<SEP>Staffs work with commanders to synchronize capabilities in congested cyberspace and electromagnetic environments.<SEP>Staffs work with commanders when planning special operations.

Protection
One of the eight elements of combat power.

Information Operations
Information operations are effectively integrated by friendly forces to influence relevant actors.<SEP>Activities conducted to isolate and degrade enemy decision-making abilities.

Soldiers
Soldiers are affected by the emotional and physical aspects of combat, including fatigue and fear.<SEP>Soldiers are affected by the effects of combat, which leaders must understand.<SEP>Soldiers require patience when achieving operational and theater strategic objectives.<SEP>Soldiers are individuals in the Army who must understand political implications and prioritize ethical conduct.

Liaison Officers
Liaison officers are used to accelerate the planning process alongside collaborative systems.

Electronic Warfare
Electronic warfare capabilities are integrated by friendly forces to the lowest possible echelons.<SEP>Activities conducted to isolate and degrade enemy decision-making abilities.

Information Environment
The information environment affects actors and military operations and requires understanding to influence behavior.

Land Domain
Tactical through strategic land operations depend on the ability of Army forces to affect behavior in this domain.

ADP 6-0
ADP 6-0 defines situational understanding as the product of applying analysis and judgment.<SEP>ADP 6-0 contains a discussion of the mission variables known as METT-TC.<SEP>ADP 6-0 contains a description of the operations process.

Combat
Combat is a lethal clash of opposing wills and a violent struggle characterized by friction, violence, and chance.

Art of Tactics
The art of tactics includes innovative application of means, decision making under uncertainty, and understanding combat effects on soldiers.

Tactics
Tactics involves the art and science of military aspects like capabilities, techniques, and procedures.<SEP>Tactics is the employment, ordered arrangement, and directed actions of forces in relation to each other.

Mission Variables
Mission variables have many combinations that make each tactical situation unique and are analyzed for situational understanding.<SEP>Mission variables are collected by commanders to make informed decisions.

Warning Orders
Warning orders are used by units to maximize parallel planning and share information with subordinates early.

Collaborative Systems
Collaborative systems are tools used alongside liaison officers to accelerate the military decision-making process.

Unit Cohesion
Unit cohesion is a critical factor that leaders must protect against the risk of collapse due to combat stress.

Military Decision-Making Process
Commanders and staffs need to master the fundamentals of this process before abbreviating it.

Local Population
The local population is one of the relevant actors whose behavior and capabilities Army forces seek to affect in the area of operations.

Tempo
Tempo refers to the speed or rhythm of the operation which commanders seek to control.

Control Measures
Control measures are arranged and chosen by commanders to manage forces and operations.

Adversaries
Adversaries are distinct from enemy forces and are among the actors whose behavior is affected by Army operations.<SEP>Opposing forces employing various weapon systems in urban environments.

Area of Operations
The area of operations (AO) is the specific region where Army forces affect the behavior and capabilities of enemies and populations.

Risk
Risk characterizes all operations involving choices and the cost of those choices.<SEP>Risk is a necessary element in formulating and executing plans, often embraced as opportunity by successful commanders.<SEP>The exposure of someone or something valued to danger, harm, or loss, inherent in every military decision.<SEP>Risk is a factor assessed continuously by Commanders and balanced against opportunities.

Advance Guards
Detached elements of a command excluded from the main body during tactical operations.<SEP>Advance Guards are detached elements of a command not included in the Main Body.

Resources
Resources are allocated by commanders as part of the forces and control measures in operations.<SEP>Resources are allocated by Commanders to minimize risk through changes.

Tactical Fundamentals
Tactical Fundamentals is the section title covering the art and science of tactics in ADP 3-90.<SEP>A section within ADP 3-90 discussing risk reduction, command decisions, and operational agility.

Main Body
The principal part of a tactical command or formation, excluding detached elements like guards.<SEP>The Main Body is the principal part of a tactical command or formation, excluding detached elements.

Tactical Command
The overall command structure of which the main body is the principal part.<SEP>A Tactical Command is a structure of which the Main Body is the principal part.

Flank Guards
Detached elements of a command excluded from the main body during tactical operations.<SEP>Flank Guards are detached elements of a command not included in the Main Body.

Covering Forces
Detached elements of a command excluded from the main body during tactical operations.<SEP>Covering Forces are detached elements of a command not included in the Main Body.

Formation
A Formation is a military organization structure of which the Main Body is the principal part.

Reserves
Reserves are forces whose size is weighed by Commanders against the disposition of the Main Body.

Security Forces
Security Forces are forces whose size is weighed by Commanders against the disposition of the Main Body.

Uncertainty
A degree of unknown factors inherent in decisions that contributes to risk and requires acceptance by commanders.<SEP>Uncertainty is a factor continually weighed by Commanders alongside information and risk.<SEP>Uncertainty characterizes tactical operations and requires commanders to balance risks with opportunities.

Task Organization
Task Organization is an element subject to changes as part of the Operations Process.

Priorities
Priorities are an element subject to changes as part of the Operations Process.

Operations Process
The operations process helps commanders drive operations and develop a common operational picture.<SEP>The Operations Process includes changes to task organization, mission, and priorities.

Mission
Mission is a specific objective for which Commanders determine optimal formation and organization.

Opportunities
Opportunities are potential benefits associated with changes, balanced against risks.

Detached Elements
Detached Elements are parts of a command, such as advance guards, that are not included in the Main Body.

Purpose
Purpose is the objective Commanders aim to achieve by balancing opportunities and risks.

Consolidate Gains
Consolidate gains involves activities to make enduring any temporary operational success and set conditions for sustainable security.

9th Armored Division
The 9th Armored Division conducted the seizure of the bridge at Remagen in March 1945.

Situation
Situation is the context that warrants changes and resource allocation by Commanders.

Operational Environment
A thorough understanding of the operational environment helps commanders develop tactical solutions.<SEP>The Operational Environment encompasses the political, military, economic, social, and other variables influencing operations.<SEP>The Operational Environment is the context commanders must understand to achieve objectives and defeat adversary forces.

Chapter 1
Chapter 1 is a section of the ADP 3-90 document containing the provided doctrine.

Hasty Operation
A hasty operation directs immediately available forces using fragmentary orders with minimal preparation.

Bridge At Remagen
The bridge at Remagen was seized by the 9th Armored Division during a hasty operation.

Seizure Of The Bridge At Remagen
The seizure of the bridge at Remagen illustrates a hasty operation conducted in March 1945.

Subordinate Leaders
Subordinate leaders execute the commander's plan and require training to master tactics.

Deliberate Operation
A deliberate operation allows the development and coordination of detailed plans including multiple branches and sequels.

Tactical Intelligence
Tactical intelligence requirements may not be satisfied in time due to the perishable nature of combat information.

1st Infantry Division
The 1st Infantry Division conducted a breaching operation during Operation Desert Storm.

Breaching Operation
The breaching operation during the opening hours of the ground phase of Operation Desert Storm illustrates a deliberate operation.

Combat Information
Combat information is unevaluated data gathered by or provided directly to the tactical commander.

Operation Desert Storm
Operation Desert Storm included a ground phase in February 1991 where deliberate operations occurred.

Planning Process
The planning process prepares branches or sequels and helps commanders resource operations.

Decision-making Process
The decision-making process must not be paralyzed by a lack of information.

JP 2-01
JP 2-01 defines combat information as unevaluated data.

Legitimate Authorities
Legitimate authorities receive transition of control after consolidating gains.

Intelligence Staff
The intelligence staff helps commanders assess combat information used in decision making.

Common Operational Picture
The common operational picture is developed by the operations process to facilitate decision making and communication.

Enemy
The opposing force whose weaknesses commanders seek to expose and whose preparations impact operational timing.<SEP>The enemy utilizes urban terrain for cover and employs various surface-to-air attacks against friendly aircraft.<SEP>The Enemy is an opposing force whose proximity to friendly forces complicates airspace planning.<SEP>Opposing force that may observe landing zones and engage aircraft.<SEP>Enemy forces may observe suitable Landing Zones and engage in activity near interchanges.<SEP>The Enemy is denied opportunities for exploitation through military government operations.

Fragmentary Orders
Fragmentary orders are used in hasty operations to direct immediately available forces with minimal preparation.

Operation
Military activities where risk cannot be avoided and must be managed to accomplish the mission.

Higher Commander
A superior leader whose intent and constraints guide the commander's decision-making process.<SEP>The higher commander sets intent and constraints that guide decision making.

Unit
A unit's combat power and tempo are reflected by momentum.

Course Of Action
A plan or option commanders consider regarding risk to the force and mission against perceived benefits.

Commander
Leaders responsible for making informed decisions, managing risk, and shaping success in military operations.<SEP>The commander whose intent and ROE understanding is imperative for mission planning and operations.<SEP>The Commander receives situational understanding and support from Civil Affairs forces and operations.

Decision
Choices made by commanders that include risk and determine the course of action within intent and constraints.

Information Technologies
Systems integrated with leaders and formations to reduce risk and facilitate decisive action.

Battalion Task Force
A tactical unit example that can conduct actions on contact without the loss of momentum.

Actions On Contact
A series of combat actions taken on contact with the enemy to develop the situation.

Security Elements
Units occupying security areas to provide early warning, protection, and initial enemy contact.

Mission Command Approach
A method used by friendly forces to achieve agility through shared understanding and estimates.

Reserve
Forces kept available to compensate for increased risk or exploit opportunities during operations.

Planning
Situational understanding and running estimates that reduce risk and inform bold decisions.

Subordinates
Personnel who collaborate with commanders to analyze risk levels and determine mitigation strategies.

Security Area
An area occupied by a unit's security elements including the areas of influence of those elements.

Strategic Level Of Warfare
The strategic level of warfare provides the context for tactical operations and goals.

Operational Level Of Warfare
The operational level of warfare provides the context for tactical operations and end states.

Agility
The ability of friendly forces to react faster than enemy forces, mitigating risk in tactical operations.

Figure 1-1
A visual representation within ADP 3-90 showing techniques available to commanders to reduce risk.

Risk Reduction
The process of mitigating risk through techniques such as planning, information gathering, or resource commitment.

Battle
A battle is a set of related engagements that lasts longer and involves larger forces than an engagement.

METT-TC
METT-TC represents mission variables including mission, enemy, terrain, weather, troops, time, and civil considerations.

Tactical Level Of Warfare
The tactical level of warfare is the level at which battles and engagements are planned and executed to achieve military objectives.

JP 3-0
JP 3-0 is a publication referenced for definitions of tactical level of warfare, engagements, and battles.

Tactical Problem
A tactical problem occurs when mission variables of the desired situation differ from the current situation.

Engagement
An engagement is a tactical conflict, usually between opposing lower echelon maneuver forces.<SEP>Engagement is a task associated with target acquisition in military operations.

TTP
Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures provide commanders and staffs with the fundamentals to develop solutions to tactical problems.

Army Leaders
Army leaders at all echelons master the art and science of tactics to solve battlefield problems.

Science Of Tactics
The science of tactics is a distinct yet inseparable concept from the art of tactics.

Art Of Tactics
The art of tactics involves the creative and flexible array of means, decision making under uncertainty, and understanding combat effects.

Brigades
Brigades are lower echelon units that generally conduct engagements.

National Assets
National assets include space-based and cyberspace capabilities that support tactical operations.

Major Operation
Major operations are affected by battles and contribute to strategic purposes.

Division
Division is an echelon that achieves significant objectives in battles.

Corps
Corps is an echelon that achieves significant objectives in battles.

Task Forces
Task forces are tactical units assigned military objectives at the tactical level of warfare.

Campaign
A campaign is affected by battles and represents a larger military operation.

Joint Capabilities
Joint capabilities are combined military capabilities that ADP 3-90 takes advantage of.

Space-Based Capabilities
Space-based capabilities are national assets that provide support to tactical operations.

Cyberspace Capabilities
Cyberspace capabilities are national assets that provide support to tactical operations.

ATP 3-06.1/MCRP 3-20.4/NTTP 3-01.04/AFTTP 3-2.29
This document is a joint publication dated 22 FEB 2022 containing guidelines on UAS categorization and operational planning.<SEP>A military publication dated 22 FEB 2022 providing guidance on urban operations and aviation considerations.<SEP>A military publication dated 22 FEB 2022 containing guidelines on urban operations, grid systems, and flight techniques.<SEP>Military manual doctrine published on 22 FEB 2022 containing guidelines for urban operations.<SEP>ATP 3-06.1/MCRP 3-20.4/NTTP 3-01.04/AFTTP 3-2.29 is a military manual dated 22 FEB 2022 providing guidance on urban operations, navigation, and landing zone considerations.<SEP>This document contains guidelines on environmental and night considerations for aircraft operations.

Man-Portable Air Defense Systems
Small, concealable systems allowing for rapid engagements against aircraft.

Antiarmor Rockets
Weapons readily available and inexpensive, normally standard equipment at small-unit levels.

Rocket-Propelled Grenades
A type of antiarmor rocket used by adversaries.<SEP>RPGs are inexpensive antiarmor rockets readily available at small-unit levels.

Commercial Off-The-Shelf SUAS
Unmanned aircraft systems that can be weaponized or modified to carry munitions.

Tank Guns
Weapons containing fire control systems effective against hovering or slow-flying helicopters.

Antitank Guided Missiles
Weapons used by adversaries containing modern fire control systems.<SEP>Antitank guided missiles are standard equipment at small-unit levels and threaten aviation assets.

Light-To-Medium Air Defense Artillery
Air defense systems employed by adversaries from ground sites or buildings.

Urban Area
The operational environment where every structure is a potential enemy position.

Buildings
Structures in urban areas that can limit radio communications and provide concealment.

Heavy Air Defense Artillery
Air defense systems requiring extended beyond LOS detection capabilities.

Surface-To-Air Missiles
Missiles employed by adversaries within urban boundaries.

Basement
A location within structures used by enemy forces for command posts to advantage concealment.

Pilots
Operators of low-flying aircraft needing awareness of fields of fire.

Aircrews
Personnel who must establish communications with ground maneuver elements.<SEP>Aircrews are personnel who should establish communications with ground elements and controlling agencies.<SEP>Aircrews are assisted by products like satellite imagery to minimize unknowns and visualize objective areas.<SEP>Personnel operating aircraft who must account for hazards and use specific insertion techniques.<SEP>Aircrews are personnel who maintain orientation using linear features and navigational systems.

Dismounted Troops
Ground forces firing at roofs of buildings, creating fields of fire.

Planners
Personnel who brief aircrews and consider civilian population issues.<SEP>Planners face unique challenges when conducting JIPOE and must consider CD concerns for SEAD operations.<SEP>Individuals responsible for selecting landing zones and planning operational details.<SEP>Planners are responsible for selecting Landing Zones and assuming enemy observation.<SEP>Planners identify, assess, and employ partners based on military commander intent and end state.

Joint Fires Observers
Personnel who should anticipate danger-close scenarios during urban operations.

Civilian Population
Non-military individuals in urban areas considered during planning for density and distinction.

Tactical Air Operations Centers
Airspace control elements using positive and procedural control methods.

JTACs
Joint terminal attack controllers acting as primary controllers for aircraft in assigned areas.

Air Officer
Officers acting as primary controllers for aircraft operating within assigned areas.

FAC(A)
Forward air controllers (airborne) acting as primary controllers for aircraft.

Joint Air-Ground Integration Center
Airspace control elements using procedural control methods beneath coordinating altitude.

Combatants
Individuals involved in fighting that must be distinguished from noncombatants.<SEP>Individuals posing a security risk to FARPs and ADGRs during refuel and rearm operations.

Noncombatants
Civilians not involved in fighting that must be distinguished from combatants.<SEP>Noncombatants are present in high concentrations in urban operations and influence planning considerations.<SEP>Noncombatants are individuals present in the urban environment near protected sites and friendly forces.

Control And Reporting Centers
Airspace control elements using positive and procedural control methods.

Pre-Mission Briefing
Briefings updating aircrews with current intelligence assessments.

Direct Air Support Center
Airspace control elements using procedural control methods beneath coordinating altitude.

Airspace Information Center
Airspace control elements using procedural control methods beneath coordinating altitude.

Army Attack Aviation
Military aviation units with specific procedure missions.

C2 Planning
Detailed, flexible, and redundant planning to alleviate electromagnetic challenges.

Combined Arms Rehearsal
Detailed rehearsals to synchronize effects in urban environments.

Air Asset Deconfliction And Integration
Processes to deconflict and integrate air assets using control methods.

Radios
Communication equipment using high-power transmissions to overcome transmission problems.

Positive Control Methods
Control methods used by airspace control elements above coordinating altitude.

Remote Antennas
Equipment used to overcome transmission problems in urban environments.

Procedural Control Methods
Control methods used by airspace control elements beneath coordinating altitude.

Natural Disasters
Events that can degrade or damage preexisting C2 networks.

Helicopters
Rotary-wing aircraft targeted by tank guns and antitank guided missiles.

Urban Operations
Military operations conducted in urban areas requiring specific planning and coordination.<SEP>Operations conducted in urban terrain requiring unique planning considerations such as aircraft deconfliction and high noncombatant concentration.

JP 3-09.3
A publication referenced for information on Close Air Support.<SEP>JP 3-09.3 is a reference document for detailed discussion on environmental conditions and weather effects on CAS.

Aircraft
Air assets including rotary-wing or tiltrotor aircraft operating in urban environments.<SEP>Aircraft operate in confined airspace and face hazards such as wires, towers, and enemy fire in urban environments.<SEP>Rotary-wing, tiltrotor, or fixed-wing vehicles used for insertion, extraction, and refueling operations.<SEP>Aircraft are aerial vehicles including rotary-wing, tiltrotor, and fixed-wing types involved in FARP and ADGR operations.

Civilian Vehicles
Vehicles on which adversaries can mount air defense artillery.

Intelligence Assessments
Current information provided to aircrews during pre-mission briefings.

ROE Constraints
Rules of engagement constraints influencing area selection for air defense employment.

Fields Of Fire
Areas from which air and ground forces fire, requiring awareness by pilots.

C2 Networks
Command and control networks that can be degraded by natural disasters.

Close Air Support
A type of military operation referenced in JP 3-09.3 for danger-close scenarios in urban operations.<SEP>Military action that requires coordination between supported units and supporting aircrews using target reference systems.

Airborne Warning And Control System
An airspace control element used to deconflict and integrate air assets above the coordinating altitude.

Radio Relay Support Systems
Systems that may overcome transmission problems associated with urban environments and C2 planning.

Fire Support Coordination Measures
Measures used effectively to plan for airspace control in high-density air traffic environments.

Air Defense Measures
Measures used effectively to plan for airspace control in high-density air traffic environments.

MGRS Coordinate System
A coordinate system that allows joint planners to efficiently produce the required Grid Reference Graphic for an entire Area of Operations.

Rooftop Retransmission Systems
Systems that may overcome transmission problems associated with vertical structures limiting radio communications.

Grid Reference Graphic
A product supported by the ground force commander used for target handover and reference, containing version numbers and contact information.

Aircrew
The Aircrew provides input to produce relevant aviation maps and charts before mission execution.<SEP>Personnel who receive target handovers and transition to reference systems used by ground elements upon arrival.<SEP>Aircrew use NVDs and must discern light sources during night formation tactics.

Ground Force Commander
The Ground Force Commander establishes the scheme of maneuver depicted on common operations graphics.<SEP>The ground force commander is normally the supported commander for urban operations.<SEP>The commander responsible for producing and disseminating the Grid Reference Graphic to supporting units and agencies.

Target Reference Point
A technique using fixed points, distance, and direction to identify targets, often coordinated for Close Air Support.

Urban Flight Techniques
Tactical approaches for flight profiles in urban areas, weighing surprise against risk of terrain or enemy fire.

Building Marking Techniques
Methods for numbering building sides, floors, and windows to give aircrews specific locations relative to structures.

Water Tower
A structure identified as TRP 002, suitable for use as a target reference point because it is easily identifiable from the air.

Joint Planners
Personnel who use the MGRS coordinate system to produce Grid Reference Graphics.

Supporting Units
Military units that receive the Grid Reference Graphic from the ground force commander.

Integrated Air Defense System
A system considered as a factor when determining flight profiles during urban operations.<SEP>Integrated Air Defense System is a threat factor to consider when determining flight profiles in urban areas.

Simple Grid System Technique
A grid technique useful when the objective area is not aligned with north-up or requires additional detail for small areas.

22 FEB 2022
22 FEB 2022 is the publication date associated with the military documents.<SEP>The publication date of the military manual ATP 3-06.1/MCRP 3-20.4/NTTP 3-01.04/AFTTP 3-2.29.<SEP>Publication date of the military manual ATP 3-06.1/MCRP 3-20.4/NTTP 3-01.04/AFTTP 3-2.29.<SEP>22 FEB 2022 is the publication date of the ATP 3-06.1 manual.

Objective Area
The specific location where operations are conducted, often requiring specific grid alignment or reference systems.

Subordinate Commands
Subordinate Commands should deconflict radio frequency assignments with frequency managers.<SEP>Military commands that receive the Grid Reference Graphic from the ground force commander.

Small Arms
Small arms are a predominant threat to aviation assets in urban environments, emplaced in supersurface locations.<SEP>Small Arms are weapons easily concealed and operated from multiple urban vantage points.<SEP>Weapons that pose a risk to aircrews, mitigated by high flight profiles.<SEP>Weapons used by the entrenched Rangers to halt enemy attacks.

Reference Areas
Areas created by intersections of roads or dominant geographical features for reference in nonlinear road structures.

CAS 9-Line
A specific excerpt format used in Close Air Support coordination using the objective area reference-grid technique.

Controlled Flight Into Terrain
A risk associated with low flight profiles during urban operations.

Joint Agencies
Agencies that receive the Grid Reference Graphic from the ground force commander.

Named Areas of Interest
Basic areas such as cloverleaves, bridges, and choke points added to graphics templates.

Operators
Personnel who use the latest update of graphics and coordinate with planners.

Tactical Surprise
A requirement commanders evaluate when determining flight profiles.

Low Flight Profiles
Flight technique that increases tactical surprise but increases risk of terrain collision.

Bridges
Examples of named areas of interest added to graphics templates.

High Flight Profiles
Flight technique that enhances enemy detection but lowers risk of small arms fire.

Issuing Organization
The organization responsible for controlling versions of the graphics and ensuring operators use the latest update.

Version Numbers
Information included in graphics to ensure control over versions and updates.

Roads
Geographical features whose intersections create reference areas.<SEP>Roads are examples of possible locations for airdrops and linear features for navigation.

Urban Environment
The Urban Environment is a dense, three-dimensional area that creates challenges for airspace control and frequency management.<SEP>City setting that creates challenges for communications and aircraft maneuvering.

Landing Zone (LZ)
Designated areas for aircraft landing, selected by planners with consideration for enemy observation and tactical feasibility.

Choke Points
Examples of named areas of interest added to graphics templates.

Rooftop
Top of a building used as a landing zone, subject to load-bearing constraints and hazards.<SEP>Rooftop is a potential landing area on load-bearing structures in urban environments.

Load-Bearing Structures
Buildings capable of accommodating helicopter landings, often requiring marking to determine capacity.

Helipads
Marked rooftop areas with known load-bearing capabilities for safe landing.

ADGR
Location type similar to FARP requiring assessment for aircraft operations.<SEP>ADGR locations require concealment from surrounding terrain and buildings to secure ground entry and exit routes.

FARP
Forward Arming and Refueling Point used for refueling and rearming aircraft.<SEP>FARP locations require concealment from surrounding terrain and buildings to secure ground entry and exit routes.

Sports Stadiums
Potential sites considered for FARP and ADGR locations to provide concealment.<SEP>Sports stadiums are considered potential sites for FARP and ADGR locations.

LOS Communications
Line of Sight communications significantly challenged by urban environments.

Rooftop Insertion and Extraction Techniques
Procedures including hovering, fast roping, and hoist operations for safe rooftop operations.

Established Airfields
Potential sites considered for FARP and ADGR locations.<SEP>Established airfields are considered potential sites for FARP and ADGR locations.

Hoist Operations
A rooftop insertion and extraction technique preferred for the evacuation of civilians.

Mechanical Turbulence
Turbulence encountered near large heating, ventilating, and air conditioning systems on building roof tops.

Tiltrotor Aircraft
Tiltrotor aircraft are involved in FARP and ADGR operations and marshalling plans.<SEP>A type of aircraft requiring marshalling plans at FARP and ADGR sites.

Light Pollution

Joint Intelligence Preparation Of The Operational Environment
JIPOE faces unique challenges in urban environments due to environmental variables and vertical development.

Air Traffic Hazards
Air traffic hazards include rotary-wing, tiltrotor, fixed-wing aircraft, and SUAS within urban areas.

Machine Guns
Machine guns are used by adversaries in urban environments to threaten friendly aircraft.

SUAS
Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems are used by friendly ground forces and present air hazards requiring integration into airspace control.<SEP>SUAS are Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems recognized as group 1 and 2 unmanned aircraft.

Environmental Hazards
Environmental hazards include meteorological effects like haze, mist, dust, and unpredictable wind effects.

Natural Hazards
Natural hazards include mountains, hills, trees, and areas with high concentrations of birds.

Physical Hazards
Physical hazards are mostly man-made obstructions like kites, antennas, wires, and power lines.

Global Positioning System
GPS is susceptible to jamming by the enemy, affecting navigation and electrical systems.

Electromagnetic Hazards
Electromagnetic hazards include high-intensity radio transmission areas and GPS jammers affecting aircraft systems.

Air Defense Artillery
Light-to-medium ADA can be employed by adversaries against friendly aircraft.

ATP 3-06.1
ATP 3-06.1 is the publication outlining general planning considerations for urban operations.<SEP>ATP 3-06.1 is a military publication referenced in the document header and footer.

AFTTP 3-2.29
AFTTP 3-2.29 is a military publication referenced in the document header and footer.<SEP>AFTTP 3-2.29 is a co-designated publication outlining general planning considerations for urban operations.

MCRP 3-20.4

NTTP 3-01.04 is a military publication referenced in the document header and footer.<SEP>NTTP 3-01.04 is a co-designated publication outlining general planning considerations for urban operations.

Improvised Explosive Devices
IEDs are surface and supersurface threats to ground forces in urban terrain.

Booby Traps
Booby traps are surface and supersurface threats to ground forces in urban terrain.

Space Operators
Space operators can provide navigational accuracy predictions and plotting of known jammer effects.

Coalition Partners
Coalition partners are recipients of releasable unclassified satellite imagery.

High-Energy Laser Pointers
High-energy laser pointers are surface and supersurface threats to ground forces in urban terrain.

Rotary-Wing
Rotary-wing aircraft are part of the high volume of air traffic within urban areas.

Marshalling Plans
Marshalling plans are designed for normal and low-light visibility conditions involving various aircraft types.

GPS-Aided Guidance Systems
GPS-aided guidance systems are not affected by terrestrial weather but accuracy is affected by storm activity.

GPS Jammers
GPS jammers are used by the enemy to cause electromagnetic hazards affecting navigation.

Solar and Geomagnetic Storm Activity
Solar and geomagnetic storm activity can affect the accuracy of GPS-aided guidance systems.

Weapon Systems
Weapon systems accuracy can be adversely affected by winds in urban areas.

Tiltrotor
Tiltrotor aircraft are part of the high volume of air traffic within urban areas.

High-Rise Rooftops
High-rise rooftops are physical hazards that can be obscured by low ceilings.

Inertial Navigation Systems
Inertial navigation systems are weapons systems not affected by weather conditions.

Weather Conditions
Weather conditions include lighting, visibility, thermal reflection, and smoke or fog affecting operations.

Urban Areas
Urban Areas are environments where ground maneuver elements use terrain-based reference systems.<SEP>Urban areas have higher temperatures and structures that affect wind patterns and IR signatures.

IR Signatures
IR signatures are affected by the proximity of buildings and higher urban temperatures.

Ceilings
Ceilings are weather conditions that can obscure hazards and deny aircraft required altitude.

Winds
Winds in urban areas are affected by city structures and disrupt low-altitude weapon accuracy.

IR Strobe Lights
IR strobe lights are marking tools whose effectiveness may be precluded by urban lighting.

NVD
NVDs are night vision devices that may be overwhelmed by urban lights.

Thermal Sights
Thermal sights are IR sensors adversely affected by thermal heating in urban environments.

Urban Lights
Urban lights are artificial lighting sources in urban areas that may overwhelm aircrew NVDs and affect IR strobe light effectiveness.

City Structures
City structures are buildings and constructions in urban areas that affect wind patterns and IR signatures.

Ground Observers
Ground observers are personnel who may detect aircraft highlighted by artificial lighting under low cloud conditions.

CAS
CAS is a close air support event that may occur simultaneously with MEDEVAC in the same airspace.<SEP>CAS (Close Air Support) is a military operation type affected by weather conditions as discussed in JP 3-09.3.

Aircraft Sensors
Aircraft sensors are systems whose performance can be degraded by reduced visibility conditions.

IR Sensors
IR sensors include thermal sights and other devices adversely affected by thermal heating in urban environments.

Thermal Reflection
Thermal reflection is an environmental concern affecting IR signatures and sensor performance.

Smoke or Fog
Smoke or fog are environmental conditions that reduce visibility and degrade sensor performance.

Power Lines
Power lines are physical hazards and obstructions that can be obscured by low ceilings.

Unguided Weapons
Unguided weapons are low-altitude weapon systems whose accuracy is adversely affected by high winds in urban areas.

Rural Areas
Rural areas are locations with generally lower temperatures compared to urban areas.

Smokestacks
Smokestacks are physical hazards and obstructions that can be obscured by low ceilings.

Lighting Conditions
Lighting conditions are environmental concerns including artificial lighting and urban lights affecting operations.

Towers
Towers are physical hazards and obstructions that can be obscured by low ceilings.

Smog
Smog is a condition causing reduced visibility that degrades aircraft sensor performance.

Dust
Dust is a condition causing reduced visibility that degrades aircraft sensor performance.

Alleys
Alleys are urban features where wind patterns are disrupted and funneled.

Rain
Rain is a condition causing reduced visibility that degrades aircraft sensor performance.

Night Formation Tactics
Night formation tactics are standard procedures that may be rendered useless by overwhelmed NVDs.

Target Acquisition
Target acquisition is a task for which unaided vision is sometimes sufficient.

Streets
Streets are urban features where wind patterns are disrupted and funneled.

Deconfliction
Deconfliction is an action requiring plan adaptation due to urban lighting effects on NVDs.

Marking Tools
Marking tools include IR strobe lights used for identification by aircrew.

Ordnance Delivery
Ordnance delivery is an aircraft task requiring sufficient time and altitude.

Environmental Concerns
Environmental concerns include weather, lighting conditions, IR signatures, visibility, thermal reflection, and smoke or fog.

Air Force
The Air Force is a military organization that refers to Groups 4 and 5 UASs as RPAs.<SEP>The Air Force is a military branch that refers to specific UAS groups as RPAs.

National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency
The National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency is a source of hazard information for geospatial products.

Air Defense Plan
The Air Defense Plan is an overall strategy into which new capabilities countering UAS systems must be integrated.<SEP>Air Defense Plan must integrate new capabilities to counter low, slow, and smaller UASs.

Unmanned Aircraft System (UAS)
Unmanned Aircraft Systems are aircraft systems that must be integrated into the overall air defense plan.

Operational Planning Products
Operational Planning Products include maps and graphics that must be discernible from ground and air perspectives.

Remotely-piloted Aircraft (RPA)
Remotely-piloted Aircraft are Groups 4 and 5 UASs operated by personnel trained to similar standards as manned aircraft pilots.

Common Operations Graphics
Common Operations Graphics depict objectives and phase lines to illustrate the ground force commander's scheme of maneuver.

UAS Categorization Chart
The UAS Categorization Chart classifies unmanned aircraft into five groups based on weight, altitude, and speed.

Route Planning
Route Planning is a process where planners must consider UAS lost-link contingency procedures.

Lost-link Contingency Procedures
Lost-link Contingency Procedures are actions taken by a UAS when communication is lost, requiring announcement over tactical chat.

Military Grid Reference System (MGRS)
The Military Grid Reference System is a technique used by joint planners to efficiently produce the required GRG.

Geospatial Products
Geospatial Products range from paper tourist maps to digital mapping databases and require continuous updates.

Gridded Reference Graphic (GRG)
The Gridded Reference Graphic is produced by overlaying a grid reference system on urban areas to identify buildings.

Tokyo Special
Tokyo Special is a datum reference system that differs from World Geodetic System 1984 and can cause position errors.

World Geodetic System 1984
World Geodetic System 1984 is the current joint standard reference system for preparing maps or charts.

Pilot
The Pilot is trained to similar standards as manned aircraft pilots and announces lost-link conditions.

Airspace Control Elements
Airspace Control Elements include systems like AWACS, TAOC, and CRC used to relay lost-link situations.

Operator
The Operator controls the UAS and should announce a lost-link condition over tactical chat.

Planner
The Planner considers UAS lost-link contingency procedures and ensures operational planning products are discernible.

Intelligence Personnel
Intelligence Personnel may have the only source of hazard information required for aviation maps.

Operations Staff
The Operations Staff shares responsibility for maintaining accurate and current geospatial products.

RQ-11B
RQ-11B is a Group 1 Unmanned Aircraft System listed in the UAS Categorization Chart.

Wasp III
Wasp III is a Group 1 Unmanned Aircraft System listed in the UAS Categorization Chart.

MQ-1 Predator
MQ-1 Predator is a Group 4 Unmanned Aircraft System listed in the UAS Categorization Chart.

MQ-9 Reaper
MQ-9 Reaper is a Group 5 Unmanned Aircraft System listed in the UAS Categorization Chart.

Group 3
Group 3 is a UAS category defined by maximum gross takeoff weight below 1,320 pounds and altitude below 18,000 feet MSL.

RQ-4 Global Hawk
RQ-4 Global Hawk is a Group 5 Unmanned Aircraft System listed in the UAS Categorization Chart.

Group 1
Group 1 is a UAS category defined by maximum gross takeoff weight of 0-20 pounds and altitude below 1,200 feet AGL.

TAOC
TAOC is an airspace control element used to relay lost-link situations.

Group 2
Group 2 is a UAS category defined by maximum gross takeoff weight of 21-55 pounds and altitude below 3,500 feet AGL.

Group 4
Group 4 is a UAS category defined by maximum gross takeoff weight below 1,320 pounds and any airspeed.

Group 5
Group 5 is a UAS category defined by maximum gross takeoff weight above 1,320 pounds and altitude above 18,000 feet MSL.

AWACS
AWACS is an airspace control element used to relay lost-link situations.

Cyberspace Domain
The Cyberspace Domain is an increasingly congested and contested environment where commanders must assure data access.

CRC
CRC is an airspace control element used to relay lost-link situations.

Notices To Airmen
Notices To Airmen are known flight hazards published by the airspace control element.

Electromagnetic Environment
The Electromagnetic Environment is a contested domain where spectrum saturation occurs in urban areas.

Airspace
Airspace is the three-dimensional region where aviation assets operate and must be controlled.

MEDEVAC
MEDEVAC is an air medical evacuation event that may occur simultaneously with close air support in the same airspace.

Frequency Management
Frequency Management is a planning method essential for voice and data spectrum users in urban environments.

Airspace Control
Airspace Control is a planning and execution method required to synchronize aviation assets and ground fires.

Cyberspace Electromagnetic Activities
Cyberspace Electromagnetic Activities are capabilities synchronized by commanders to support unified land operations.

Unified Land Operations
Unified Land Operations are supported by planned and integrated cyberspace and electromagnetic warfare operations.

Unmanned Aircraft System
Unmanned Aircraft System is a general category of aircraft that includes SUAS and RPAs.

RPA
RPA are Remotely-Piloted Aircraft referred to by the Air Force as groups 4 and 5 UASs.

Ground Control Stations
Ground Control Stations are equipment used to operate SUAS, often with limited waypoint programming.

Civilian Aircraft
Civilian Aircraft may be present in airspace following natural disasters without military communication.

Government Aircraft
Government Aircraft may be present in airspace following natural disasters without military communication.

Radio Frequency
Radio Frequency availability can be reduced in urban areas due to public safety and commercial usage.

Aviation Assets
Aviation Assets are aircraft resources that must be synchronized with ground fires into the ground scheme of maneuver.

Ground Maneuver Elements
Ground Maneuver Elements are military units with which aircrews should establish communications.

Area Frequency Manager
Area Frequency Manager is an entity with which subordinate commands should deconflict radio frequency assignments.

Controlling Agencies
Controlling Agencies are entities with which aircrews should establish communications before crossing airspace boundaries.

Table 2
Table 2 contains information about UAS categories referenced in the document.

Forward Arming and Refueling Points
Forward Arming and Refueling Points (FARPs) are locations considered when selecting assembly or holding areas.

Regional Frequency Manager
Regional Frequency Manager is an entity with which subordinate commands should deconflict radio frequency assignments.

Rally Points
Rally Points are used for in-flight contingencies in urban terrain.

Holding Areas
Holding Areas are used for in-flight contingencies and should avoid loitering at low altitudes.

Landing Zones
Landing Zones (LZs) are locations considered when selecting assembly or holding areas for helicopters.

Full-Motion Video
Full-Motion Video (FMV) flight paths are used to alert friendly ground forces of impending dangers.

Air-Delivered Ground Refueling Sites
Air-Delivered Ground Refueling (ADGR) sites are locations considered when selecting assembly or holding areas.

Infrared Pointer
Infrared (IR) pointer usage is a communication procedure to alert friendly ground forces.

Assembly Areas
Assembly Areas are selected using considerations similar to LZs, FARPs, and ADGR sites.

Air Tasking Order
Air Tasking Order is used for deconfliction and synchronization of aviation assets.

Public Safety
Public Safety usage reduces radio frequency availability in urban areas.

Airspace Control Plan
Airspace Control Plan is used for deconfliction and synchronization of aviation assets.

Airspace Control Order
Airspace Control Order is used for deconfliction and synchronization of aviation assets.

Navigation Waypoints
Navigation Waypoints are programmed into SUAS ground control stations, often limited to four or less.

Risk Assessment
Risk Assessment is a factor to consider when determining flight profiles to mitigate potential dangers.

Laser Pointers
Laser Pointers are devices easily concealed and operated from multiple urban vantage points.

Flight Profiles
Flight Profiles are determined by factors including tactical mission, risk assessment, terrain relief, and threat density.

MANPADS
MANPADS are weapons easily concealed and operated from multiple urban vantage points.

Urban Navigation
Urban Navigation involves techniques and systems used to navigate over large towns and cities effectively.

SAMs
SAMs are weapons easily concealed and operated from multiple urban vantage points.

RPGs
RPGs are weapons easily concealed and operated from multiple urban vantage points.

GPS
GPS is a technology used to reduce problems associated with night navigation and orientation.

Aircraft Survivability Equipment
Aircraft Survivability Equipment is a factor considered when determining flight profiles.

Parks
Parks are examples of possible locations for airdrops and suitable landing zones in major cities.

IR Pointers
IR Pointers are markers used to reduce problems associated with orientation and target identification.

Laser Target Designators
Laser Target Designators are devices used to reduce problems associated with orientation and target identification.

Drop Zone
Drop Zone refers to sites for airdrop operations in urban terrain requiring extensive planning.

Linear Features
Linear Features include highways, rivers, and railways that provide recognizable boundaries for navigation.

Stadiums
Stadiums are examples of possible locations for airdrops and suitable landing zones.

AH-1/64
AH-1/64 is an aircraft type requiring a 100x100 feet single ship landing zone size.

H-60
H-60 is an aircraft type requiring a 100x100 feet single ship landing zone size.

Commercial Aviation
Commercial Aviation usage reduces radio frequency availability in urban areas.

Landing Zone
Landing Zone refers to areas selected for helicopter and tiltrotor landing requiring specific size considerations.

A/OH-6, H-6
A/OH-6 and H-6 are aircraft types requiring a 65x65 feet single ship landing zone size.

Table 3
Table 3 outlines helicopter and tiltrotor landing zone size considerations and requirements.

CV-22
CV-22 is a tiltrotor aircraft requiring a 240x240 feet landing zone size.

MV-22
MV-22 is a tiltrotor aircraft requiring a 200x200 feet landing zone size in visual conditions.

H-47
H-47 is an aircraft type requiring a 120x120 feet single ship landing zone size.

H-53
H-53 is an aircraft type requiring a 200x300 feet single ship landing zone size.

UH-1
UH-1 is an aircraft type requiring a 100x75 feet single ship landing zone size.

Airfields
Airfields are examples of possible locations for airdrops in urban terrain.

Industrial Storage Sites
Industrial Storage Sites are examples of possible locations for airdrops in urban terrain.

Golf Courses
Golf Courses are potential Landing Zones in major cities.

Railroad Yards
Railroad Yards are examples of possible locations for airdrops in urban terrain.

Cultural Lighting
Cultural Lighting is a challenge in urban terrain affecting navigation.

Parking Lots
Parking Lots are potential Landing Zones in major cities.

Audible Signature
Audible Signature is a factor to consider when determining flight profiles.

Rotor Wash
Rotor Wash is a hazard associated with certain aircraft types like H-47 and H-53.

LOS Interference
LOS Interference is a challenge in urban terrain affecting navigation.

GPS and Spectrum Jamming
GPS and Spectrum Jamming are challenges in urban terrain affecting navigation.

Maps
Maps provide a foundation for choosing Landing Zones but are not sufficient alone.

Reconnaissance Assets
Reconnaissance Assets produce products used to examine terrain for Landing Zones.

Imagery
Imagery is reviewed to accurately assess Landing Zone size and hazards.

Brown-out Conditions
Brown-out Conditions are anticipated hazards for MV-22 operations affecting landing zone size.

LZ Planning Guide
LZ Planning Guide is a reference document for Landing Zone size requirements.

Load-bearing Structures
Load-bearing Structures are buildings that can accommodate helicopters landing on their rooftop.

Ground Photos
Ground Photos provide valuable information and terrain references for Landing Zone assessment.

Unaided Vision
Unaided vision is sufficient for some portions of target acquisition.

Foreign Humanitarian Assistance
Foreign humanitarian assistance is an assigned special operations activity conducted by special operations forces.<SEP>Foreign Humanitarian Assistance is limited in scope and duration to relieve human suffering and is defined in JP 3-29.

Civil Affairs Operations
Civil Affairs Operations are executed through four core competencies to support commanders and integrate civil knowledge.<SEP>Civil affairs operations are an assigned special operations activity executed through core competencies like civil network development.<SEP>Civil Affairs Operations are activities conducted by Army special operations forces.

Department Of State
The Department Of State is a federal agency mentioned in relation to leading agency societies and referenced in JP 3-26.

Department Of Defense
The Department Of Defense issues directives that limit Army involvement in counterterrorism and conducts activities outside the United States.<SEP>The Department of Defense establishes counterproliferation policy and works with USSOCOM on weapons of mass destruction efforts.<SEP>The U.S. government department responsible for security cooperations and force assistance activities.

Department Of Justice
The Department Of Justice is a federal agency mentioned in relation to leading agency societies and referenced in JP 3-26.

Direct Action
Direct Action is a specific activity conducted by Army Special Operations Forces.<SEP>Direct action is an assigned special operations activity conducted by special operations forces.<SEP>Direct Action consists of high-risk, low-visibility short-duration strikes and small-scale offensive actions defined in JP 3-05.

528th Sustainment Brigade
The 528th Sustainment Brigade provides temporary support to humanitarian assistance efforts and enables international organizations.<SEP>528th Sustainment Brigade provides planners integrated into a Special Forces group planning team.<SEP>The 528th Sustainment Brigade is one of the only Army special operations forces elements capable of providing Role 2 level care.

Special Forces
Special Forces are units that employ infantry tactics and conduct direct action operations.<SEP>Special Forces units lived and worked with partners in the Philippines as part of JSOTF-P special operations activities.

Ranger Units
Ranger Units are units that employ infantry tactics and conduct direct action operations alongside Special Forces.

Civil Affairs Units
Civil Affairs Units can establish civil-military operations centers to coordinate partner institutions.

Civil-Military Operations Center
The Civil-Military Operations Center coordinates partner institutions and gathers information to prioritize restoring basic services.<SEP>A civil-military operations center is a mechanism established by Civil Affairs forces to coordinate activities and share information.

United States
The United States established JSOTF-P as part of the Global War on Terror and maintains a partnership with the Philippines.<SEP>The United States is the country where Department of Defense activities are conducted outside of for humanitarian assistance.<SEP>The United States is a nation whose military forces and partners engage in unconventional warfare and special operations.<SEP>The United States is the country whose interests are impacted by threats and protected by security cooperations.<SEP>The nation whose security interests and foreign policy are supported by security cooperations.

Joint Special Operations Task Force-Philippines
The Joint Special Operations Task Force-Philippines (JSOTF-P) was established in 2002 to advise and assist the Armed Forces of the Philippines in combating terrorist groups.<SEP>The Joint Special Operations Task Force-Philippines was established in 2002 as part of broader U.S. efforts.

Philippines
The Philippines is the host nation where JSOTF-P operated and where the Comprehensive Agreement on Bangsamoro was implemented.<SEP>The Philippines is the location associated with the Joint Special Operations Task Force.

JP 3-26
JP 3-26 is a publication referencing the Department of Justice and Department of State.<SEP>JP 3-26 is a joint publication referenced in relation to counterterrorism definitions.

JP 3-05
JP 3-05 is a document referenced for the definition of special reconnaissance.<SEP>JP 3-05 is a publication defining Direct Action operations.<SEP>JP 3-05 is a joint publication defining unconventional warfare.<SEP>JP 3-05 is a joint publication referenced regarding hostage rescue and operational preparation of the environment.

JP 3-29
JP 3-29 is a publication defining Foreign Humanitarian Assistance.

Counterterrorism
Counterterrorism involves activities to neutralize terrorists and their networks to prevent violence and coercion.<SEP>Counterterrorism is an assigned special operations activity conducted by special operations forces.<SEP>Counterterrorism is an area where Army involvement is limited by Department of Defense directives.

JP 3-22
JP 3-22 is a publication defining Foreign Internal Defense.

Foreign Internal Defense
Foreign Internal Defense is a specific activity conducted by Army Special Operations Forces.<SEP>Foreign internal defense is an assigned special operations activity conducted by special operations forces.<SEP>Foreign Internal Defense involves activities to assist a partner government in addressing internal threats and is defined in JP 3-22.<SEP>Activities that overlap with security force assistance to build host-nation capacity against threats.

ATP 3-05.2
ATP 3-05.2 provides details on how Army forces enable host nation forces to maintain internal stability.

Intelligence Operations
Intelligence Operations are a specific activity conducted by Army Special Operations Forces.<SEP>Intelligence Operations are a specific activity conducted by Army special operations forces.

Internal Stability
Internal Stability is a goal enabled by Army special operations forces within host nations.

Host Nation
The Host Nation refers to the partner government or country receiving assistance or defense support.<SEP>The host nation whose forces are enabled by Army forces to maintain internal stability.<SEP>The target nation where security force assistance operations are conducted to develop capability.

Hostage Rescue And Recovery
Hostage Rescue And Recovery is a specific activity conducted by Army special operations forces.

Military Information Support Operations
Military Information Support Operations are a specific activity conducted by Army Special Operations Forces.<SEP>Military information support operations are an assigned special operations activity and a designated skill for USASOC.<SEP>Military Information Support Operations are operations to influence the behavior of targeted foreign audiences in support of a commander's objectives.<SEP>Military Information Support Operations are a specific activity conducted by Army special operations forces.<SEP>Military Information Support Operations are employed in conjunction with influence efforts to dissuade adversary reliance on weapons of mass destruction.

U.S. Forces
U.S. Forces provide foreign humanitarian assistance limited in scope and duration.

Security Force Assistance
Security force assistance is a directed special operations activity.<SEP>Security Force Assistance is a specific activity conducted by Army special operations forces.<SEP>Efforts to assess, assist, generate, employ, and sustain operational capability in host nations.

Sensitive Material Recovery
Sensitive Material Recovery is a specific activity conducted by Army special operations forces.

Sensitive Site Exploitation
Sensitive site exploitation is a designated skill for which USASOC serves as the lead special operations component.<SEP>Sensitive Site Exploitation is a specific activity conducted by Army special operations forces.

26 June 2025
The publication date of FM 3-05.<SEP>26 June 2025 is the publication date listed on FM 3-05.<SEP>The date associated with the FM 3-05 document header.

Host Nation Civil Authorities
Host Nation Civil Authorities have the primary responsibility for providing assistance in their country.

International Organizations
International Organizations arrive to provide humanitarian assistance enabled by U.S. units.<SEP>International Organizations are part of the complex interorganizational environment involving partners working towards mutual security objectives.

Host-Nation Security Forces
Host-Nation Security Forces are assessed, trained, advised, and assisted by Army special operations forces.

2002
The year the Joint Special Operations Task Force-Philippines was established.<SEP>2002 is the year the Joint Special Operations Task Force-Philippines was established.

Anti-Ship Operations
Anti-Ship Operations are tactics conducted by Special Forces and Ranger units during direct action.

Sabotage
Sabotage is a tactic conducted by Special Forces and Ranger units during direct action.

Sniping
Sniping is a standoff attack included in direct action operations.

Insurgency
Insurgency is an internal threat countered by foreign internal defense operations.

Terrorism
Terrorism is an internal threat countered by foreign internal defense operations.<SEP>Terrorism is a security threat countered by U.S. Army counter threat finance activities.

Subversion
Subversion is an internal threat countered by foreign internal defense operations.

Personnel Recovery
Capability required to plan and conduct recovery of personnel or sensitive equipment during special operations.

Mines
Mines are munitions emplaced by Special Forces and Ranger units.

Security Cooperation
Security cooperation is a directed special operations activity.<SEP>Security cooperation involves Department of Defense interactions with foreign security establishments to build relationships and promote security interests.<SEP>Interactions with foreign security establishments to build relationships and promote U.S. security interests.

Precision-Guided Munitions
Precision-Guided Munitions receive terminal guidance from Special Forces and Ranger units.

An article by T.E. Lawrence published in Army Quarterly in 1920.

T.E. Lawrence
Author quoted in Chapter 4 regarding the fundamentals of special operations.

Special Operations
Military activities that require personnel recovery capability and follow specific principles and imperatives.

Army Quarterly
A publication that featured T.E. Lawrence's article in 1920.

Joint Force
Joint force commanders are supported by USASOC and conventional forces conduct irregular warfare activities as part of joint force efforts.<SEP>The military force that security force assistance helps to produce competent foreign security forces for.<SEP>The Joint Force is an entity whose operations are supported by Army special operations forces tasks and missions.

Security entities in partner nations that receive assistance and training.

Army Tenets Of Operations
Foundational principles for Army special operations forces to plan and conduct operations.

FM 3-22
A referenced document providing detailed discussion on support to security cooperation.

Partner Nations

U.S. Special Operations Forces Schools
Educational institutions where foreign security force personnel are sent for training.

Unconventional Assisted Recovery

Survival, Escape, And Evasion
Methods in which all Army special operations forces personnel are trained.

Internal Defense And Development Program
Program emphasized during security force assistance to address root causes of instability preventively.

Search And Rescue
Capability for which select Army special operations forces are trained and equipped.

Chapter 2
Chapter 2 provides an overview of special operations activities that Army special operations forces plan and execute.<SEP>A chapter in FM 3-05 covering Special Operations Forces Personnel Recovery.

Army Special Operations Principles
Principles of partnership, integration, and persistence that serve as the foundation for special operations.

Abu Sayyaf
Abu Sayyaf is an Al-Qaeda-linked terrorist group primarily combated by JSOTF-P.

Chapter 4
A chapter in FM 3-05 exploring Fundamentals of special operations.<SEP>Chapter 4 is the section of FM 3-05 covering Army special operations principles.

Armed Forces of the Philippines
The Armed Forces of the Philippines received advice and assistance from JSOTF-P to combat terrorist groups.

Al-Qaeda is linked to terrorist groups such as Abu Sayyaf and Jemaah Islamiyah that were targeted by JSOTF-P.

Indo-Pacific Command
The Indo-Pacific Command utilizes the partnership and presence in the Philippines as contributions to its campaign plan.

The Secretary of Defense has the authority to approve directed special operations activities.<SEP>The Secretary of Defense requires reporting on all activities conducted under military information support operations authorities.

Titled Army Special Operations Activities, the document serves as the primary source outlining doctrine related to Army Special Operations activities. It encompasses a broad range of military topics, including unconventional warfare, special operations principles, and civil affairs operations. The manual details the fundamentals and limitations of Army special operations forces, establishing the foundational knowledge required for these units.

The publication is organized into chapters, with Chapter 2 specifically outlining Army special operations activities. Beyond structural details, FM 3-05 contains doctrine on Army special operations principles as well as Army and Special Operations imperatives, providing guidance on operational conduct. Additionally, the field manual document contains references to events involving the Ranger company, integrating specific operational examples or historical contexts within its doctrinal framework. Through these components, FM 3-05 functions as a comprehensive guide for the forces it governs.
